title.en: Hainuwele: The Coconut Girl and the DEMA Creation of the Kei Islands
title.zh: 海努韋萊：椰子之女與凱伊群島之德瑪創世

region.zh: 印尼馬魯古群島凱伊群島

summary.en: Ameta, hunting wild pigs, finds a coconut in a boar's tusk; a girl, Hainuwele, grows from it in three days bearing valuables in her palms; at the maro dance the men crowd around her until she sinks into the ground; Ameta digs up her body and cuts it into pieces, which, buried, become the clans' food-plants — the dema myth of culture rising from murder.
summary.zh: 阿梅塔獵野豬，於豬牙中得椰子；三日期間椰中生出女孩海努韋萊，掌中藏寶；瑪羅舞會上眾男擁擠相擠，少女陷入地中；阿梅塔掘其屍，碎而埋之，化為各氏族之食用植物——此為『德瑪』神話：文化自謀殺中生。

narrative.en:
Hainuwele is the best-known dema myth — the 'dema' (ancestral-deity) narratives of Maluku recorded by the Frobenius Institute expedition of 1937-38 under Adolf E. Jensen — in which the world's culture rises from the killing of a primordial being.

BEGINNING: THE COCONUT IN THE TUSK. Ameta, the hunter of the Kei Islands, was tracking a wild pig; the boar's tusk held a coconut — an object unknown in the land. He brought it home and put it in a basket; after three days a girl emerged from the coconut: Hainuwele, 'the coconut branch? the coconut girl'. In the hollows of her palms she bore valuables — porcelain dishes? gold? gongs and gift-goods — for the household: she is the source of wealth.

MIDDLE: THE MARO DANCE AND THE SINKING. At the great maro dance (the nine-night exchange festival), Hainuwele stood at the center of the dancing circle, giving gifts from her palms. Each night the men pressed closer around her; on the ninth night, the circle closed — the men crowded around her 'like the? like? ' — and she sank into the ground and was gone. (In the variants, the men's greed for her gifts is the cause; the dema's death is collective.)

END: THE PIECES THAT BECAME FOOD. Ameta dug her up and, instructed by a spirit (or following the custom), cut her body into pieces and buried them at the dance ground. From the buried pieces grew the plants: yams, taro, coconuts, tubers — each piece a food, distributed among the clans (each clan's staple from a different part). Jensen's theory: the dema narratives encode the theology that human culture (agriculture, ritual, death) rises from the primordial murder of the dema-being — killing is the price of sustenance, and ritual (the maro dance, the funeral) re-enacts it. The corpus of dema myths around Hainuwele (the Maro dance cycle, the Watumas? the primordial sisters) frames the Kei understanding of death, planting, and exchange.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Kei agriculture (clans' staple plants from the dema's body), the maro festival (gift-exchange as re-enactment), the theology of death (burial as planting), and the comparative typology of dismembered-culture myths (Purusha, Ymir — with the distinction that the dema is killed collectively and produces not the cosmos but the food system). Provenance: the Jensen expedition (1937-39, Dutch East Indies) recorded with named informants in the notebooks; colonial-era — flagged; contemporary Maluku scholarship (e.g. Kei community publications) is preferred.
narrative.zh: 海努韋萊為馬魯古『德瑪』（祖靈神）神話之最著名者，1937-38 年弗羅貝尼烏斯研究所遠征隊（詹森主持）採錄。獵人阿梅塔追野豬，於豬牙中得椰子——此物前所未有；帶回家置於籃中，三日後椰中生出女孩海努韋萊；其掌紋中藏寶物（瓷器、金、鑼與禮品），為家宅之財源。九夜瑪羅交換節之舞會上，海努韋萊立於舞圈中央施贈；夜夜眾男逼近，第九夜圍擠——少女陷入地中而失（變體言因眾男貪其贈禮；德瑪之死屬集體）。阿梅塔掘其屍，依神諭（或依俗）碎而埋於舞場；埋處生出薯蕷、芋、椰、塊莖——每一片成一種食物，分歸各氏族（各氏族之主食自不同部位）。詹森之論：德瑪神話之神學即人類文化（農耕、儀式、死亡）自原始謀殺中生——殺戮為取食之代價，儀式（瑪羅舞、葬禮）即其重演。凱伊人圍繞海努韋萊之德瑪敘事群（瑪羅舞循環、原始姊妹瓦圖瑪斯等）構成其對死亡、種植與交換之理解。功能：氏族主食之釋義、瑪羅節之憲章、葬為種之死亡神學、以及碎身造物神話比較類型（普魯沙、尤彌爾——惟德瑪為集體所殺、所產非宇宙而為食物體系）。

functions: Aition of agriculture: clans' staple plants from the dema's buried body
Charter of the maro festival: gift-exchange as ritual re-enactment
Theology of death: burial as planting; the funeral as planting rite
Comparative typology: the dismembered-culture myth in its Indonesian form

title.en: Bathala Maykapal: The Tagalog Creation and the Three Rivals
title.zh: 巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾：他加祿創世與三神之爭

region.en: Luzon (Tagalog region; symbolic pin at Manila)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋島他加祿地區（象徵性定位於馬尼拉）

texts.period: Recorded early 20th c.: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain); Fay-Cooper Cole, The Tinguian, Chicago 1922

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain), 'The Creation' and 'The Battle of the? ' Tagalog sections; Fay-Cooper Cole, The Tinguian, 1922

summary.en: Bathala Maykapal, ruler of the sky, wars with Aman Sinaya of the sea and Amihan of the northeast wind; Amihan, tiring of the battle, flies between them, and the sky-god's thrown rock and the sea-goddess's islands meet — the Philippine archipelago is born, and from a bamboo stalk the first man and woman emerge.
summary.zh: 天神巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾與海神阿曼·西納亞及東北風之神阿米漢相爭；阿米漢厭戰，飛於二者之間；天神擲石、海神起島，相遇成群島——菲律賓由是而生；竹節中走出最初之男女。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the 1916 Cole collection (American colonial-era; flagged); Philippine IPRA law (1997) vests community intellectual rights over indigenous knowledge.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Cole (1916), 'The Creation' (Tagalog): Bathala of the sky, Aman Sinaya of the sea, and Amihan of the northeast wind quarreled; Bathala threw great rocks at the sea-goddess, and she raised great waves; Amihan, weary of the war, flew between them — the rocks fell where she passed and became islands. Not verbatim.

Not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales, Chicago 1916 (public domain); Damiana L. Eugenio, Philippine Folk Literature: The Myths, Quezon City 1993 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE THREE POWERS. The Tagalog creation narrative recorded by Cole (1916) begins with three primordial powers: Bathala Maykapal ('Maker' Bathala), ruler of the sky; Aman Sinaya, goddess of the sea; and Amihan, the bird-shaped deity of the northeast wind. The sky and the sea warred: Bathala hurled great rocks at the sea-goddess; she answered with towering waves; the battle shook the world.

MIDDLE: THE WIND BETWEEN. Amihan, the northeast wind, weary of the eternal battle, flew between the two antagonists — and where the wind passed, Bathala's thrown rocks could not fall into the sea but struck the shallow waters and stood as islands: 'and thus were the islands of the Philippines formed.' The peace-making wind is the aition of the archipelago — seven thousand islands as projectiles arrested mid-fall.

END: THE BAMBOO AND THE FIRST COUPLE. On one of the islands a bamboo stalk grew tall; it split, and from one half came the first man Malakas ('Strong') and from the other the first woman Maganda ('Beautiful'); they married and bore children — in the fuller folk telling the children scatter (the blind? the shy ones hide in the house walls — ancestors of the hidden peoples; the wanderers go to sea — ancestors of? ), grounding the diversity of Philippine peoples. Bathala remains the supreme sky-father (the term 'Bathala' itself became the Tagalog word for God in Christian translation), the ancestral pantheon's head, whose helpers (the anito? the katutubong anito) mediate between him and the people.

RITUAL WORLD. Bathala's worship in the pre-colonial Tagalog world was mediated by the babaylan (priestesses, often women or feminized men) who offered to the anito — carved ancestral spirits housed in the household and the fields; the diwata of the groves and the? the river spirits received offerings of rice wine, betel, and first-fruits at the village pag-aanito rites. The narrative's three powers map onto this ritual division: the sky-father above, the sea beneath the fisher's world, the wind of the monsoon that opens and closes the sailing year — the agricultural and maritime calendar of Luzon written as divine politics. The bamboo couple grounds the household itself: the first house, the first fire, the division of labor between Malakas and Maganda as the folk explanation of marriage custom. Under Spanish rule the name Bathala transferred to the Christian God (the Doctrina Christiana of 1593 uses Bathala for Deus), making the creation narrative the hinge between the old anito religion and Philippine Catholicism — one reason the story remains the country's most recognizable myth.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Tagalog cosmology (sky-sea duality settled by wind), the aition of the archipelago (islands as thrown rocks), the bamboo-couple origin of humanity, and the term 'Bathala' as the theological bridge to colonial Christianity; it is the best-known Philippine myth nationally (school textbooks), collected in the American colonial era (Cole 1916 — flagged) and re-collected by Eugenio's Philippine Folk Literature series.
narrative.zh: 他加祿創世（科爾1916年採錄）：太初有三神——天神巴哈拉·馬伊卡帕爾、海神阿曼·西納亞、東北風神阿米漢。天海相戰：巴哈拉擲巨石，海神起巨浪，世界震動。阿米漢厭於永戰，飛於二者之間——風過之處，天神所擲之石不得落海深處，立於淺水而成島嶼：『菲律賓群島由是而成』——七千島即半途受阻之飛石。其中一島生巨竹，竹裂，上半出首男馬拉卡斯（『強』），下半出首女馬甘達（『美』）；結為夫婦生子，子孫分散（躲於牆內者為隱匿族群之祖、漂於海上者為航海者之祖），釋菲島民族之多樣。巴哈拉為最高天父（Bathala 一詞後成他加祿語中『神』之稱，為基督教譯名之橋）。功能：天海二元經風而和之宇宙觀、群島飛石釋義、竹節男女之人類起源、以及國家教科書中之民族敘事。

functions: Aition of the archipelago: islands as sky-god's thrown rocks arrested by wind
Bamboo-couple origin: Malakas and Maganda as national first ancestors
Theological bridge: 'Bathala' as the Tagalog name of God in Christian translation
National school-canon: the best-known Philippine creation narrative
